intro.text: When Rehoboam refused to lighten Solomon's yoke, the northern tribes answered “What portion have we in David?” and made Jeroboam king; “there was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only”.

This guide counts nineteen kings of Israel, from Jeroboam I to Hoshea, in the order Kings gives them. Tibni, whom half the people followed against Omri, is left out of the count because Kings gives him no reign of his own.

Kings dates every northern king by the reign of the king of Judah, and Judah's kings by Israel's. Chronicles gives no record of its own for any king of Israel; they appear there only in Judah's story.
Of the nineteen, seven were killed by the man who took the throne (Nadab, Elah, Joram, Zechariah, Shallum, Pekahiah and Pekah), and Zimri died in the burning palace when Omri took Tirzah.

Kings condemns seventeen of them, most in the words “did evil in the sight of the LORD”; Jehu's verdict is mixed, and Shallum, who reigned a month, is given none. Almost every verdict adds that the king did not depart from “the sins of Jeroboam”.
The kingdom ended when “the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria”; Kings explains the fall at length.
Dates are scholars' reconstructions, not Scripture. Each reign shows Thiele's system as revised by McFall and Young (the main system), and Ussher's traditional dates of 1658.

verdictNotes.text: Ahijah's message to him: “thou hast not been as my servant David” but “hast done evil above all that were before thee”.
His sin becomes the measure for later kings of Israel, almost all of whom “departed not from the sins of Jeroboam”.
Kings' closing account of the north names him: “Jeroboam drave Israel from following the LORD, and made them sin a great sin”.
Chronicles adds that he and his sons cast the Levites off from the priest's office, and that he ordained priests “for the high places, and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made”.

accession.text: While he was in charge of the labour of “the house of Joseph”, Ahijah the Shilonite tore a new garment into twelve pieces and gave him ten: “I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee”.
Ahijah promised him “a sure house, as I built for David”, if he would walk in God's ways.
Solomon sought to kill him, and he fled to Shishak king of Egypt until Solomon died.
When Rehoboam refused to lighten the yoke, Israel answered “What portion have we in David?” and made Jeroboam “king over all Israel”; only Judah followed the house of David.
Kings gives the cause: “the cause was from the LORD, that he might perform his saying, which the LORD spake by Ahijah the Shilonite”.

events.label: Golden calves at Beth-el and Dan

claim.text: Fearing that worship at Jerusalem would turn the people back to Rehoboam, he made two calves of gold, saying “behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt”, and set one in Beth-el and the other in Dan.

events.label: New priests and a new feast

claim.text: He made priests “of the lowest of the people, which were not of the sons of Levi”, and a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, “the month which he had devised of his own heart”.

events.label: The man of God at the altar

claim.text: A man of God from Judah cried against the altar at Beth-el and named a future king, “Josiah by name”; Jeroboam's hand dried up when he stretched it out against him, and was restored when the man prayed.
When his son Abijah fell sick, his disguised wife went to Ahijah at Shiloh; Ahijah foretold the end of Jeroboam's house, and the child died as she reached the threshold at Tirzah.
“There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days.”
Chronicles tells of a battle in Abijah's reign: Jeroboam's 800,000 against Judah's 400,000 by mount Zemaraim; Israel lost 500,000 men, and Abijah took Beth-el, Jeshanah and Ephrain.
“Neither did Jeroboam recover strength again in the days of Abijah: and the LORD struck him, and he died.”

worship.text: Two golden calves, at Beth-el and Dan; “this thing became a sin: for the people went to worship before the one, even unto Dan”.
A “house of high places”, priests not of Levi, and a feast of his own in the eighth month.
The priests and Levites left their lands for Judah and Jerusalem, followed by those “such as set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel”.

building.text: Shechem in mount Ephraim, then Penuel.

alliances.text: Scripture records no treaty or tribute in his reign; his one foreign tie is his time in Shishak's Egypt before he became king.

people.text: The northern tribes' complaint was the “grievous service” and “heavy yoke” of Solomon.
Rehoboam's tax officer Adoram was stoned by “all Israel”, and Israel “rebelled against the house of David unto this day”.

claim.text: Promised him ten tribes, and later sent his wife home with the sentence on his house.

Stopped Rehoboam's war to win back the north: “this thing is from me”.

claim.text: He married Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, served Baal, and built an altar for Baal in “the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria”.
“In his days” Hiel the Beth-elite built Jericho at the cost of his eldest and youngest sons, as Joshua had said.
Elijah: “there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word”.
Jezebel “cut off the prophets of the LORD”; Obadiah, over Ahab's house, hid a hundred of them in caves.
Elijah called Israel and the 450 prophets of Baal to Carmel; fire fell on his offering, the people cried “The LORD, he is the God”, the prophets of Baal were killed at the Kishon, and the rain came.
Ben-hadad and thirty-two kings besieged Samaria; following a prophet's word, Ahab's young men routed them.
At the return of the year the Syrians fought in the plain by Aphek; a man of God promised victory, and Ben-hadad surrendered.
Ahab spared Ben-hadad, who promised to restore cities and give him streets in Damascus: “So he made a covenant with him, and sent him away.”
A prophet in disguise told him: “thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people”.
Naboth refused to sell his inheritance; Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name, Naboth was stoned, and Ahab went to take the vineyard, where Elijah met him.
“They continued three years without war between Syria and Israel.”
With Jehoshaphat of Judah he went up to take Ramoth-gilead from Syria, against Micaiah's warning, and was killed there.

Mesha says that after Omri “his son succeeded him; and he also said, I will afflict Moab”, and that Israel held Medeba “during his days, and half his son’s days, forty years”. The son is not named.

first.text: Kings tells the story and ends with the dogs licking his blood at the pool of Samaria.

second.text: Chronicles tells it almost word for word, adds that when Jehoshaphat cried out “the LORD helped him; and God moved them to depart from him”, and ends with Ahab's death at sunset.

questions.question: Who led Damascus at Qarqar, and is he the Ben-hadad of 1 Kings 20?

views.label: Hadad-ezer
views.holders: D. D. Luckenbill (1926), §611

argument.text: Luckenbill translates the name of the Damascus king on the Monolith as “Hadad-ezer, of Aram”.

views.label: Bir-idri, that is Ben-hadad
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912), p. 296, note 1, following Delitzsch, Winckler and (later) Zimmern

argument.text: Rogers reads “Bir-idri” and says “He is the king who is called Benhadad in 1 Kings 20”; he notes that Schrader, Zimmern and Ungnad had read the name “Adad-idri or Hadad-idri”.

questions.question: When did Moab break free: in Ahab's reign or after his death?

views.label: After Ahab's death
views.holders: 2 Kings 1:1 and 3:5; A. H. Sayce, ISBE (1915), p. 2072

argument.text: Kings says “Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab”; Sayce takes the stele's “forty” as “an indefinite period of time” and writes that “the revolt of Mesha took place after Ahab's death”.

views.label: In the middle of Ahab's reign
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1890), pp. lxxxix and xciv

argument.text: Driver reads the stele's “half his son’s days” as Ahab's and concludes the revolt “took place in the middle of Ahab's reign, not after his death (as stated, 2 Ki. 1, 1)”.

notSaid: The Bible does not mention the battle of Qarqar or Ahab's part in it; that is known only from Shalmaneser's monolith.
Scripture gives no age for Ahab and does not name his mother.
Kings names “the ivory house” and “all the cities that he built” but does not say where they were.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: His capital; the house of Baal; his burial

rulers.name: Ahaziah

identifications.text: Ahaziah son of Ahab, king of Israel; not Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah (2 Kings 8:24), who died at Jehu's hands.

synchronism.text: Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah

verdict.text: he did evil in the sight of the LORD

verdictNotes.text: “He served Baal, and worshipped him, and provoked to anger the LORD God of Israel, according to all that his father had done.”
Chronicles calls him the king “who did very wickedly”.

accession.text: “Ahab slept with his fathers; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his stead.”

quote.text: the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah

claim.text: “Then Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.”
Kings: he asked to send his servants with Jehoshaphat's ships, “But Jehoshaphat would not”.
He fell through a lattice in his upper chamber in Samaria and sent to ask Baal-zebub the god of Ekron whether he would recover.
Elijah met the messengers: “Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron?”
Two captains sent to bring Elijah were consumed by fire from heaven; the third pleaded for his life, and Elijah went down with him to the king.
He died as Elijah had said, and “Jehoram reigned in his stead ... because he had no son”.

worship.text: He served Baal and sent to Baal-zebub of Ekron.

building.text: Chronicles: ships made at Ezion-geber, to go to Tarshish, jointly with Jehoshaphat.

alliances.text: Chronicles: Jehoshaphat “join himself with Ahaziah king of Israel”.

claim.text: Sent by the angel of the LORD to meet his messengers, then to the king himself.

quote.text: thou shalt not come down off that bed on which thou art gone up, but shalt surely die

claim.text: Prophesied against Jehoshaphat for joining with Ahaziah; the ships were broken.

quote.text: Because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah, the LORD hath broken thy works

claim.text: Moab rebelled after Ahab's death; Kings names its king Mesha in the next reign's account.
He sent to enquire of Baal-zebub, “the god of Ekron”.

first.text: Kings: Jehoshaphat's ships were broken at Ezion-geber; when Ahaziah offered to send his servants with them, “Jehoshaphat would not”.

second.text: Chronicles: Jehoshaphat joined Ahaziah to make the ships, Eliezer prophesied against it, and “the ships were broken”.

questions.question: Did Ahaziah's two years overlap his father's reign?

views.label: Yes, as his father's deputy
views.holders: James Ussher, Annals of the World (1658), p. 47

argument.text: Ussher writes that Ahab, in Jehoshaphat's seventeenth year, “joyned his son Achazia with him in the rule of the kingdom, or rather made him his Vice-Roy”.

views.label: Yes, Ahab's last year was Ahaziah's first
views.holders: Edward Mack, ISBE (1915), vol. 1, p. 640

argument.text: Mack holds that “the last year of Ahab, in which came the defeat at Karkar, was the 1st of Ahaziah”.

views.label: No real overlap; the count explains the two years
views.holders: R. C. Young's tables (Thiele as revised)

argument.text: Young dates Ahaziah 853 to 852 BC, after Ahab's death in 853, and counts his “two years” by Israel's non-accession reckoning (one year elapsed).

notSaid: Scripture gives no age, mother's name or burial place for Ahaziah of Israel.
Kings does not say how Moab's rebellion went in his reign.

rulers.name: Joram
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Twelve years; the last king of Omri's house.

capital.name: Samaria
capital.note: He went to Jezreel to recover from his wounds and was killed there.

identifications.text: Kings calls him both “Jehoram” and “Joram”; at the same time Jehoram (Joram) son of Jehoshaphat reigned in Judah.

2 Kings 5–8 speaks only of “the king of Israel” (Naaman's letter, the Syrian raids, the siege of Samaria, the Shunammite's land). These chapters stand between Joram's accession (3:1) and his death (9:24); Scripture does not name the king in them.

synchronism.text: Jehoram the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah

verdict.text: he wrought evil in the sight of the LORD; but not like his father, and like his mother

comparison.text: he cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat

death.text: Jehu “smote Jehoram between his arms, and the arrow went out at his heart”; his body was cast into the plot of Naboth the Jezreelite.

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
Traditional (Ussher, 1658)

verdictNotes.text: “He put away the image of Baal that his father had made.”

accession.text: “Jehoram reigned in his stead ... because he had no son.”

quote.text: in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah
the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah
in the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel
In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel did Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah begin to reign
in the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab began Ahaziah to reign over Judah

claim.text: With Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom he marched through the wilderness of Edom against Mesha; Elisha promised water, Moab was beaten back, and at Kir-haraseth Mesha offered his eldest son on the wall; “there was great indignation against Israel” and they went home.
The king of Syria sent Naaman with a letter; “the king of Israel” tore his clothes, and Elisha said “let him come now to me”.
Elisha warned “the king of Israel” of the Syrian camps “not once nor twice”; the band sent to Dothan was struck blind, led into Samaria and sent home fed.
Ben-hadad besieged Samaria until mothers ate their children; the king wore sackcloth and swore to kill Elisha; the Syrians fled in the night, as Elisha had foretold.
“The king” heard from Gehazi what Elisha had done and restored the Shunammite woman's land.
With Ahaziah of Judah he fought Hazael at Ramoth-gilead; “the Syrians wounded Joram”, and he went to Jezreel to be healed.
Meeting Jehu “in the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite”, he asked “Is it peace, Jehu?” and was shot as he fled.

worship.text: He removed the image of Baal his father made, but “cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam”.

alliances.text: Jehoshaphat joined his war on Moab: “I am as thou art, my people as thy people”.
Ahaziah king of Judah fought beside him at Ramoth-gilead and visited him in Jezreel.

people.text: During the siege an ass's head sold “for fourscore pieces of silver” and a woman cried to the king on the wall.
Four lepers at the gate found the Syrian camp empty and brought the news.

claim.text: Answered the three kings in the Moab campaign “were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat”; warned of Syrian raids; foretold the end of the famine; sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu.

quote.text: What have I to do with thee? get thee to the prophets of thy father, and to the prophets of thy mother

claim.text: Jehu cast Joram's body on Naboth's plot as the fulfilment of the LORD's word against Ahab.
“Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster” who had paid tribute to Israel and rebelled.
Ben-hadad besieged Samaria; Hazael smothered him and became king, and Joram fought Hazael at Ramoth-gilead.
“The king of Edom” marched with Israel and Judah against Moab.

outside.name: Tel Dan stele, Israel Museum
outside.date: About 840 BC; fragments found in 1993 and 1994

claim.text: An Aramaic inscription from Tel Dan whose speaker, an Aramaean king, claims to have killed a “king of Israel” and a king of “the house of David”; Biran and Naveh restore the damaged names as Joram son of Ahab and Ahaziah son of Jehoram.
Mesha tells how he took towns from Israel, among them Ataroth, Nebo and Yahaz (Jahaz), and fortified them; the stele does not name the Israelite king he fought after Omri's son.

questions.question: Did Joram begin in Jehoshaphat's eighteenth year (2 Kings 3:1) or in the second year of Jehoram of Judah (2 Kings 1:17)?

views.label: Both: Jehoram of Judah was already co-regent
views.holders: James Ussher (1658), p. 47; Edward Mack, ISBE (1915), p. 640; R. C. Young's tables

argument.text: All three reckonings make Jehoram of Judah king alongside his father Jehoshaphat, so the same year was Jehoshaphat's eighteenth and Jehoram's second; Ussher calls it making him “Vice-Roy”, Mack “coregency”, and Young dates it from 854 BC.

questions.question: Who killed Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah?

views.label: Jehu
views.holders: 2 Kings 9

argument.text: Kings says Jehu shot Joram and had Ahaziah struck down near Ibleam.

views.label: The Aramaean king of the Tel Dan stele
views.holders: The stele's speaker, as read by Biran and Naveh (1995)

argument.text: The Tel Dan inscription's speaker claims he killed the king of Israel and the king of the house of David. The two records are shown side by side; neither is used here to correct the other.

questions.question: Did Ahaziah of Judah begin in Joram's twelfth year (2 Kings 8:25) or his eleventh (2 Kings 9:29)?

views.label: Deputy in the eleventh, king in the twelfth
views.holders: James Ussher (1658), p. 49

argument.text: Ussher says Jehoram of Judah, being sick, made Ahaziah his “Vice-roy” in Joram's eleventh year, and that Ahaziah succeeded him in Joram's twelfth year.

views.label: Two ways of counting the same year
views.holders: R. C. Young's tables (Thiele as revised)

argument.text: Young's table gives both verses the same date, 841 BC, treating “twelfth” as Israel's non-accession count of what is the eleventh year by accession counting.

notSaid: Kings gives no “rest of the acts” note and no burial for Joram; his body was left on Naboth's plot.
Scripture does not say which king of Israel is meant in the stories of 2 Kings 5–8.
Kings gives no age for him and no mother's name in his record; Jehu speaks of “thy mother Jezebel” (2 Kings 9:22).

places.name: Jezreel
places.note: Where he recovered and was killed

rulers.name: Jehu
otherNames: Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Twenty-eight years in Samaria, after ending the house of Ahab.

identifications.text: Called “Jehu the son of Nimshi” and “Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi”.
Not the prophet Jehu son of Hanani (1 Kings 16:1), and his father Jehoshaphat is not Jehoshaphat king of Judah.

verdict.text: Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD God of Israel with all his heart

comparison.text: from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, Jehu departed not from after them

sourcesCited.text: the rest of the acts of Jehu, and all that he did, and all his might, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
Traditional (Ussher, 1658)

verdictNotes.text: The LORD's word to him: “thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes ... thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel”.
But “he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam”: the golden calves at Beth-el and Dan stayed.
Hosea, in a later reign: “I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu”.
Kings notes the promise kept when his great-great-grandson Zechariah was killed: “And so it came to pass.”

accession.text: At Horeb Elijah was told: “Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel”.
Elisha sent one of the sons of the prophets to Ramoth-gilead with a box of oil; he anointed Jehu in an inner room and fled.
The captains spread their garments under him on the stairs, blew trumpets and said “Jehu is king”; then “Jehu ... conspired against Joram”.

quote.text: In the seventh year of Jehu Jehoash began to reign

claim.text: Anointed by a young prophet sent from Elisha.
He drove “furiously” to Jezreel and shot Joram in Naboth's plot.
He had Ahaziah of Judah struck “at the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam”; Ahaziah fled to Megiddo and died there.
Jezebel was thrown from a window at Jezreel, and dogs ate her body, as Elijah had said.
By letters to Samaria he had the seventy sons of Ahab killed, their heads sent to Jezreel.
He killed forty-two brothers of Ahaziah at the shearing house.
He took Jehonadab son of Rechab into his chariot: “Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD”.
He called a great sacrifice for Baal “in subtilty”, killed the worshippers in the house of Baal, burned its images and made the house a draught house: “Thus Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel.”
“In those days the LORD began to cut Israel short”: Hazael struck all Gilead east of the Jordan, from Aroer by the Arnon, Gilead and Bashan.

worship.text: Baal destroyed out of Israel; the calves at Beth-el and Dan kept.

building.text: The house of Baal broken down and made “a draught house unto this day”.

alliances.text: Jehonadab son of Rechab rode with him to Samaria.

people.text: The rulers of Samaria answered his letter, “We are thy servants ... we will not make any king”.
East of the Jordan Israel lost “all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites”.

claim.text: Was told to anoint Jehu; Jehu cites Elijah's word at Jezebel's death and over Ahab's house.
Sent the young prophet with the oil.

person.name: The young prophet
person.note: One of the sons of the prophets, unnamed

claim.text: Anointed him and gave him the charge against the house of Ahab.

quote.text: I have anointed thee king over the people of the LORD, even over Israel

claim.text: Later, in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, Jehu's great-grandson, he named his son Jezreel as a sign against Jehu's house.

quote.text: I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu

claim.text: Hazael struck Israel in all its coasts east of the Jordan.
Shalmaneser III records receiving Jehu's tribute in his eighteenth year.
When Ahaziah was dead, his mother Athaliah “destroyed all the seed royal” and reigned.

outside.date: Shalmaneser's 18th year: 841 BC in Young's tables (Mack, 1915: 842)

outside.date: Shalmaneser's 18th year (841 BC in Young's tables)

Its Aramaean speaker claims the deaths of a king of Israel and a king of “the house of David” that 2 Kings 9 attributes to Jehu.

twoAccounts.topic: The death of Ahaziah of Judah

first.text: Kings: struck in his chariot near Ibleam, he “fled to Megiddo, and died there”; his servants carried him to Jerusalem.

second.text: Chronicles: Jehu “sought Ahaziah: and they caught him, (for he was hid in Samaria,) and brought him to Jehu: and when they had slain him, they buried him”.

first.text: Kings: Jehu met “the brethren of Ahaziah” at the shearing house and killed forty-two men.

second.text: Chronicles: he found “the princes of Judah, and the sons of the brethren of Ahaziah” and killed them.

questions.question: Why does Assyria call Jehu “son of Omri”, when Scripture makes him son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi?

views.label: “Son of Omri” as a dynastic label
views.holders: D. D. Luckenbill (1926), §§590, 672

argument.text: Luckenbill translates the phrase “Jehu, son of Omri” (Assyrian mar Humri); Assyrian texts also call Israel “Humri”, so the phrase names the realm, not Jehu's father.

views.label: “Of the land of Omri”
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912), p. 304, note 2, following Bezold

argument.text: Rogers translates “Jehu, of the land of Omri” and notes that mar Humri, “formerly translated ‘son of Omri,’ means rather ‘the people of the land of Omri’”.

notSaid: Kings does not mention any tribute from Jehu to Assyria; that is known from Shalmaneser's records.
Kings gives no cross-date for Jehu's own accession; the dating comes from Judah's Jehoash, who began “in the seventh year of Jehu” (2 Kings 12:1).
Scripture gives no age or mother's name for Jehu.

places.note: Ahaziah of Judah struck near the ascent of Gur

rulers.name: Jehoahaz
rulers.title: King of Israel

identifications.text: Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel; not Jehoahaz (Shallum) son of Josiah, king of Judah (2 Kings 23:30).

synchronism.text: In the three and twentieth year of Joash the son of Ahaziah king of Judah Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD

comparison.text: followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom

sourcesCited.text: the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
Traditional (Ussher, 1658)

verdictNotes.text: Even after relief, “they departed not from the sins of the house of Jeroboam ... and there remained the grove also in Samaria”.

accession.text: “Jehoahaz his son reigned in his stead.”

quote.text: In the three and twentieth year of Joash the son of Ahaziah king of Judah

claim.text: The LORD “delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael, all their days”.
“Jehoahaz besought the LORD, and the LORD hearkened unto him: for he saw the oppression of Israel.”
“The LORD gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians.”
He was left only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand footmen; the king of Syria had made them “like the dust by threshing”.

worship.text: The sins of Jeroboam continued, and “the grove” remained in Samaria.

people.text: After the saviour came, “the children of Israel dwelt in their tents, as beforetime”.
“Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.”

claim.text: Elisha had wept before Hazael, foreseeing “the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel”.
Hazael and then his son Ben-hadad held Israel down “all their days”.

notSaid: Scripture does not name the “saviour” of 2 Kings 13:5.
Scripture gives no age or mother's name for Jehoahaz, and Chronicles does not mention him.

rulers.name: Jehoash
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Sixteen years; three victories over Syria and one over Judah.

identifications.text: Kings calls him both “Jehoash” and “Joash”; his contemporary in Judah was Joash (Jehoash) son of Ahaziah, a different king.

synchronism.text: In the thirty and seventh year of Joash king of Judah began Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz to reign over Israel in Samaria

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD

comparison.text: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel sin: but he walked therein

death.text: “Joash slept with his fathers; and Jeroboam sat upon his throne.”

burial.text: Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel

sourcesCited.text: his might wherewith he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
Traditional (Ussher, 1658)
dates.note: Joined to his father's rule in the year of the world 3163; dies 3179 (Annals, pp. 51–52)

verdictNotes.text: Kings gives his closing formula twice, once after his accession (13:12-13) and again after the war with Amaziah (14:15-16).

accession.text: “Joash his son reigned in his stead.”

quote.text: In the thirty and seventh year of Joash king of Judah
In the second year of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel reigned Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah
Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah lived after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel fifteen years

claim.text: He wept over the dying Elisha, “O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof”; Elisha had him shoot an arrow east and strike the ground, and he struck three times.
He “took again out of the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael the cities” lost by his father: “Three times did Joash beat him”.
Amaziah of Judah challenged him, “let us look one another in the face”; he answered with the parable of the thistle and the cedar in Lebanon.
He defeated Judah at Beth-shemesh, took Amaziah, broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, and took the gold and silver of the temple and the king's house, and hostages.
Chronicles: Amaziah had hired a hundred thousand men of Israel for a hundred talents but sent them home at a man of God's word; they raided Judah's cities “from Samaria even unto Beth-horon”.

worship.text: He walked in the sins of Jeroboam.

alliances.text: Chronicles: Israel's soldiers hired by Amaziah of Judah.

people.text: “The bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year.”
“The LORD was gracious unto them ... because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

claim.text: On his deathbed promised victory over Syria, limited to three because the king struck only three times.

quote.text: The arrow of the LORD’s deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria

claim.text: Told Amaziah not to take Israel's army with him: “the LORD is not with Israel”.
Hazael died and Ben-hadad his son reigned; Jehoash beat him three times.
Amaziah lived fifteen years after Jehoash died.
Adad-nirari III (805–782 BC in Luckenbill's dating) lists “Humri (Omriland, Israel)” among the lands he brought to submission and taxed, and says he shut up the king of Aram in Damascus.

Adad-nirari says he brought “Tyre, Sidon, Humri (Omriland, Israel), Edom, Palastu” to submission and imposed tribute and tax. It names no king of Israel; this research has not tied it to a year of Jehoahaz or Jehoash.

first.text: Kings: Amaziah's heart was lifted up after his victory over Edom, and he would not hear.

second.text: Chronicles adds that Amaziah had set up the gods of Edom, and that his refusal “came of God ... because they sought after the gods of Edom”; the treasure was found “with Obed-edom”.
Chronicles tells of the hundred thousand Israelites hired and dismissed, and their raid on Judah.

notSaid: Scripture gives no age or mother's name for Jehoash of Israel.
Kings does not say which cities he recovered from Ben-hadad.

rulers.name: Jeroboam II
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Forty-one years in Samaria; Israel's borders restored.

identifications.text: Jeroboam son of Joash; Kings calls him simply “Jeroboam”. “II” is a modern label to tell him from Jeroboam son of Nebat.

synchronism.text: In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel began to reign in Samaria

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD

comparison.text: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin

death.text: “Jeroboam slept with his fathers, even with the kings of Israel; and Zachariah his son reigned in his stead.”

sourcesCited.text: how he recovered Damascus, and Hamath, which belonged to Judah, for Israel, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?

verdictNotes.text: Yet “the LORD said not that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven: but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash”.
Amos's recorded word is against “the house of Jeroboam”; the priest Amaziah reported it as “Jeroboam shall die by the sword”. Kings says Jeroboam “slept with his fathers” and that his son was killed.

accession.text: “Jehoash slept with his fathers ... and Jeroboam his son reigned in his stead.”

quote.text: In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah
In the twenty and seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel began Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah to reign
in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel
in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel

claim.text: “He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the LORD ... by the hand of his servant Jonah”.
The book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel told “how he recovered Damascus, and Hamath, which belonged to Judah, for Israel”.
The tribes east of the Jordan “were reckoned by genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel”.
Amaziah the priest of Beth-el reported Amos to the king and told Amos to flee to Judah: “it is the king’s chapel, and it is the king’s court”.

worship.text: Beth-el remained “the king’s chapel”; Amos foretold that “the high places of Isaac shall be desolate”.

people.text: “The LORD saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter: for there was not any shut up, nor any left, nor any helper for Israel.”

claim.text: Foretold the restoration of Israel's borders.

quote.text: according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher

claim.text: Prophesied in his days, “two years before the earthquake”, and was reported to him by Amaziah the priest.

quote.text: I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword

claim.text: Dates his word to the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah “and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel”.
Kings says he “recovered Damascus” for Israel.
He began in Amaziah's fifteenth year; Azariah began in his twenty-seventh.

questions.question: Azariah began “in the twenty and seventh year of Jeroboam” (2 Kings 15:1), though Jeroboam began in Amaziah's fifteenth year and Amaziah reigned twenty-nine. How do the numbers fit?

views.label: Counted from a partnership with his father
views.holders: James Ussher (1658), pp. 52–53

argument.text: Ussher counts Jeroboam's years “from the time that he began to reign in consortship with his father”, which he puts in the year of the world 3168 (836 BC).

views.label: A co-regency from 793 BC
views.holders: R. C. Young's tables (Thiele as revised)

argument.text: Young starts Jeroboam's forty-one years at a co-regency in 793 BC, eleven years before Jehoash died.

views.label: Uzziah's own co-regency
views.holders: Edward Mack, ISBE (1915), vol. 1, pp. 639–640

argument.text: Mack instead overlaps Judah's kings: Uzziah was made king after Amaziah's defeat by Jehoash, so that 15 of Amaziah's 29 years ran alongside Uzziah's.

notSaid: Kings gives no age, mother's name or burial place for Jeroboam II.
Chronicles mentions him only once, in the genealogies (1 Chronicles 5:17).
Kings does not say when or how he took Damascus and Hamath.

places.name: Hamath
places.note: “The entering of Hamath” (2 Kings 14:25) was his northern border; Kings says he recovered Hamath

places.name: Bethel
places.note: “The king’s chapel”, where Amos was opposed

rulers.name: Zechariah
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Six months; the last king of Jehu's house.

identifications.text: The KJV spells him “Zachariah”. He was the last king of Jehu's line, not the last king of Israel (Hoshea was).

synchronism.text: In the thirty and eighth year of Azariah king of Judah did Zachariah the son of Jeroboam reign over Israel in Samaria six months

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done

comparison.text: he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin

death.text: “Shallum the son of Jabesh conspired against him, and smote him before the people, and slew him.”

sourcesCited.text: the rest of the acts of Zachariah, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
dates.note: From Elul (about September) 753 to Adar (about March) 752 BC

dates.label: Traditional (Ussher, 1658)
dates.note: Year of the world 3232, after an eleven-year gap following Jeroboam's death (Annals, pp. 55–57)

verdictNotes.text: His death completed the promise to Jehu: “Thy sons shall sit on the throne of Israel unto the fourth generation. And so it came to pass.”

accession.text: “Zachariah his son reigned in his stead.”

quote.text: In the thirty and eighth year of Azariah king of Judah

claim.text: Shallum son of Jabesh conspired and killed him “before the people”.

worship.text: He did evil “as his fathers had done”.

people.text: He was killed “before the people”.

claim.text: Had foretold the sword against the house of Jeroboam.

quote.text: I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword

questions.question: Was there a gap between Jeroboam II's death and Zechariah's reign?

views.label: Yes, about eleven years
views.holders: James Ussher (1658), pp. 55–57

argument.text: Ussher finds that comparing the two kingdoms requires “an Interregnum, or vacancie of a king, in the land of Israel” of eleven years and a half, so that Zechariah's six months fall in Uzziah's thirty-eighth year.

views.label: No gap
views.holders: R. C. Young's tables (Thiele as revised)

argument.text: Young counts Jeroboam's forty-one years from a co-regency beginning in 793 BC, so his death in 753 BC leads straight to Zechariah.

notSaid: Scripture gives no age, mother or burial for Zechariah.
Kings does not say where he was killed beyond “before the people”.

rulers.name: Shallum
rulers.title: King of Israel

identifications.text: Shallum son of Jabesh, king of Israel. His father Jabesh is not said to have reigned; and he is not Shallum son of Josiah of Judah (Jeremiah 22:11).

synchronism.text: Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the nine and thirtieth year of Uzziah king of Judah

death.text: “Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah, and came to Samaria, and smote Shallum ... and slew him.”

sourcesCited.text: the rest of the acts of Shallum, and his conspiracy which he made, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
dates.note: One month, Adar to Nisan (about March to April) 752 BC

dates.label: Traditional (Ussher, 1658)
dates.note: His month falls in Uzziah's thirty-ninth year; Menahem follows in 772 (Annals, pp. 56–57)

verdictNotes.text: Kings gives Shallum no verdict at all, the only king of Israel without one.

accession.text: He “conspired against” Zechariah, “smote him before the people, and slew him, and reigned in his stead”.

quote.text: in the nine and thirtieth year of Uzziah king of Judah

claim.text: He ended the house of Jehu.
Menahem came up from Tirzah and killed him in Samaria.

people.text: He struck Zechariah down “before the people”.

notSaid: Kings gives Shallum no verdict, and no age, mother or burial.
No prophet is recorded as speaking to or about Shallum.

rulers.name: Menahem
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Ten years in Samaria; tribute to Assyria.

identifications.text: Pul, who came against the land in his reign (2 Kings 15:19), is identified with Tiglath-pileser III; see the question below.

synchronism.text: In the nine and thirtieth year of Azariah king of Judah began Menahem the son of Gadi to reign over Israel

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD

comparison.text: he departed not all his days from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin

death.text: “Menahem slept with his fathers; and Pekahiah his son reigned in his stead.”

sourcesCited.text: the rest of the acts of Menahem, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
Traditional (Ussher, 1658)

accession.text: He came up from Tirzah, killed Shallum in Samaria, “and reigned in his stead”.

quote.text: In the nine and thirtieth year of Azariah king of Judah

claim.text: He killed Shallum in Samaria.
He struck Tiphsah and its coasts from Tirzah “because they opened not to him”, and ripped up its pregnant women.
“Pul the king of Assyria came against the land: and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand.”
He raised it from “all the mighty men of wealth, of each man fifty shekels of silver”; the king of Assyria “turned back, and stayed not there in the land”.

worship.text: He did not depart “all his days” from Jeroboam's sins.

alliances.text: A thousand talents of silver to the king of Assyria to secure his throne.

people.text: Fifty shekels from each wealthy man.
The people of Tiphsah, who would not open to him.

claim.text: “Pul the king of Assyria came against the land.”

outside.name: Annals of Tiglath-pileser III
outside.date: Undated in the text; Mack (1915) put Menahem's tribute in 738 BC

claim.text: A list of kings who paid tribute includes “Menihimmu (Menahem) of Samerina (Samaria)” beside Rezin of Aram and Hiram of Tyre (Luckenbill); Rogers's translation of the same list also names Menahem of Samaria.
A broken passage reads, in Luckenbill's translation with his own question mark: “As for Menahem(?), terror overwhelmed him, like a bird, alone he fled and submitted to me.”

questions.question: Is “Pul the king of Assyria” (2 Kings 15:19) the same as Tiglath-pileser?

views.label: Yes: Pulu was his Babylonian name
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912), p. 308; the site's person data

argument.text: Rogers writes that the new king “was proclaimed under the name and style of Tiglathpileser in Assyria, and later under the name of Pulu in Babylonia”. The site's person data files 2 Kings 15:19 under Tiglath-pileser.

views.label: The KJV wording reads as two kings
views.holders: 1 Chronicles 5:26 (KJV)

argument.text: The KJV of 1 Chronicles 5:26 has “the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away” — two names, one verb in the singular.

notSaid: Scripture gives no age, mother or burial for Menahem.
Kings does not give the year of his reign in which Pul came.

places.name: Tiphsah
places.note: Struck because it would not open to him

rulers.name: Pekahiah
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Two years; killed in his own palace.

synchronism.text: In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD

comparison.text: he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin

death.text: Pekah his captain, with Argob, Arieh and fifty Gileadites, killed him “in the palace of the king’s house”.

sourcesCited.text: the rest of the acts of Pekahiah, and all that he did, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
Traditional (Ussher, 1658)

accession.text: “Pekahiah his son reigned in his stead.”

quote.text: In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah

claim.text: Pekah son of Remaliah, “a captain of his”, with fifty men of Gilead, killed him in Samaria.

worship.text: He kept to Jeroboam's sins.

people.text: His killers included “fifty men of the Gileadites”.

notSaid: Scripture gives no age, mother or burial for Pekahiah, and no event of his reign except his death.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: His capital, where he was killed

rulers.name: Pekah
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Twenty years; Assyria takes Galilee and Gilead.

synchronism.text: In the two and fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD

comparison.text: he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin

death.text: “Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah, and smote him, and slew him.”

sourcesCited.text: the rest of the acts of Pekah, and all that he did, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
dates.note: Rival reign from 752 BC; sole king 740/739 to 732/731

dates.label: Traditional (Ussher, 1658)

accession.text: As Pekahiah's captain he killed him in the palace, “and reigned in his room”.

quote.text: In the two and fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah
In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel began Jotham the son of Uzziah king of Judah to reign
In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah Ahaz the son of Jotham king of Judah began to reign

claim.text: He killed Pekahiah with fifty Gileadites.
“In those days the LORD began to send against Judah Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah.”
Rezin and Pekah “came up to Jerusalem to war: and they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him”.
Chronicles: Pekah “slew in Judah an hundred and twenty thousand in one day”; Israel carried away two hundred thousand captives to Samaria.
At Oded's word, leaders of Ephraim clothed, fed and anointed the captives and brought them to Jericho.
Tiglath-pileser took “Ijon, and Abel-beth-maachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria”.
Hoshea son of Elah conspired against him and killed him.

worship.text: He kept to Jeroboam's sins.

alliances.text: Isaiah: “Syria is confederate with Ephraim”; Rezin and “the son of Remaliah” planned to set “the son of Tabeal” as king in Judah.

people.text: The north and Gilead went into captivity in Assyria.
The tribes east of the Jordan were carried to “Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan”.

claim.text: Told Ahaz not to fear “the two tails of these smoking firebrands”, Rezin and Remaliah's son.

quote.text: the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son

claim.text: Met Israel's returning army at Samaria and had them release the captives of Judah.

quote.text: deliver the captives again, which ye have taken captive of your brethren

claim.text: Rezin was his partner against Judah until Assyria took Damascus and “slew Rezin”.
Ahaz sent silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser, who went up against Damascus.

Tiglath-pileser says he carried off to Assyria “the land of Bit-Humria” (the house of Omri), “all of its people”, and that “Pakaha, their king they deposed and I placed Ausi’ (Hoshea) over them as king” (Luckenbill); Rogers: “As Pekah, their king, they had deposed, Hosea I established as king over them.” A broken passage says that Samaria was left alone; who left it is uncertain in the damaged text (Luckenbill: “he(?)”).

first.text: Kings: Rezin and Pekah “besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him”.

second.text: Chronicles: Ahaz was “delivered into the hand of the king of Israel, who smote him with a great slaughter”.

questions.question: How does Pekah have twenty years when Menahem and Pekahiah ruled for twelve of the same years?

views.label: He ruled in Gilead first
views.holders: Edward Mack, ISBE (1915), vol. 1, pp. 639–640

argument.text: Mack: “in the confusion which followed the death of Jeroboam, Pekah established his authority” over the land east of the Jordan, and the numbers of 2 Kings 15:27, 32 and 16:1 count from that year.

views.label: A rival reign counted from 752 BC
views.holders: R. C. Young's tables (Thiele as revised)

argument.text: Young's table shows Pekah's reign overlapping Menahem's and Pekahiah's from 752 BC and his sole reign from 740/739.

views.label: Twenty years, then a gap
views.holders: James Ussher (1658), pp. 58–64

argument.text: Ussher gives Pekah twenty full years, 759–739 BC, and places a nine-year “Anarchy” after his death before Hoshea reigned quietly.

notSaid: Scripture gives no age, mother or burial for Pekah.

Kings does not mention Assyria in Pekah's fall; Tiglath-pileser's annals say “they deposed” him and that Tiglath-pileser set Hoshea over them (see Outside the Bible). Neither record makes the other wrong.

rulers.name: Hoshea
rulers.title: King of Israel
rulers.tagline: Nine years; the last king of Israel.

identifications.text: Hoshea son of Elah, the last king of Israel; not the prophet Hosea son of Beeri, and his father Elah is not King Elah son of Baasha.

synchronism.text: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah began Hoshea the son of Elah to reign in Samaria over Israel nine years

verdict.text: he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him

death.text: Kings says only that “the king of Assyria shut him up, and bound him in prison”.

dates.label: Thiele, as revised by McFall and Young
dates.note: 732/731 BC to the fall of Samaria in 723

dates.label: Traditional (Ussher, 1658)
dates.note: Kills Pekah in the year of the world 3265 (739 BC); reigns quietly from 3274; Samaria taken in 3283 (Annals, pp. 64–68)

verdictNotes.text: Kings' long explanation of the fall begins “For so it was, that the children of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God”.
“Yet the LORD testified against Israel, and against Judah, by all the prophets, and by all the seers.”
“So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day.”

accession.text: “Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah ... and slew him, and reigned in his stead, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.”

quote.text: in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah
In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah
in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, that Hezekiah the son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign
in the fourth year of king Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel
in the sixth year of Hezekiah, that is the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria was taken

claim.text: He conspired against Pekah and killed him.
“Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria; and Hoshea became his servant, and gave him presents.”
He “sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and brought no present to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year”.
“The king of Assyria shut him up, and bound him in prison.”
Shalmaneser came up against Samaria in Hoshea's seventh year and besieged it three years.
“In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.”
The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim to the cities of Samaria; they “feared the LORD, and served their own gods”.

worship.text: Kings lists the nation's sins: high places, images and groves, “two calves”, the host of heaven, Baal, children passed through the fire.

alliances.text: Tribute to Assyria, then a turn to So king of Egypt.

people.text: Israel was carried to Halah, Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes.
Chronicles: Hezekiah later sent letters to “the remnant of you, that are escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria”; many mocked, but some of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun came to Jerusalem.

claim.text: Prophesied into Hezekiah's reign and spoke of Israel's kings and the end of Samaria's king.

quote.text: As for Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water

claim.text: Had said that “within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people”.
Kings names Shalmaneser as the king who came against Hoshea and besieged Samaria; Sargon is named in Scripture only at Isaiah 20:1.
Hoshea sent messengers to “So king of Egypt”.

outside.name: Tiglath-pileser III, annals
outside.date: The 730s BC (Hoshea's accession: 732/731 in Young's tables)

claim.text: “Pakaha, their king they deposed and I placed Ausi’ (Hoshea) over them as king. 10 talents of gold, x talents of silver, as their tribute I received from them” (Luckenbill).
For 725, 724 and 723 the list notes campaigns “against [Samaria]”; the place name is broken and restored by the editor (Luckenbill's brackets).

outside.name: Babylonian Chronicle 1
outside.date: Reign of Shalmaneser V, five years by the chronicle's count

claim.text: The chronicle says, in its entry for Shalmaneser's accession, that he ravaged Samaria (Grayson's edition).

outside.name: Sargon II's annals and display inscription
outside.date: Sargon's first years (722–720 BC in Rogers)

claim.text: Sargon claims: “I besieged and captured Samaria, carrying off 27,290 of the people who dwelt therein”, took fifty chariots, and set his officers over the rest.

questions.question: Did Hoshea begin in Jotham's twentieth year (2 Kings 15:30) or in Ahaz's twelfth (2 Kings 17:1)?

views.label: He killed Pekah, then reigned after years of disorder
views.holders: James Ussher (1658), pp. 64–65

argument.text: Ussher has Hoshea kill Pekah in 739 BC, “yet by reason of stirs and tumults” unable to enjoy the throne in “a kinde of Anarchy, for the space of 9 years”, and then begin “quietly to reign in the later end of the 12 year of Achaz”.

views.label: Different starting points in Judah
views.holders: R. C. Young's tables (Thiele as revised)

argument.text: Young dates Hoshea from 732/731 BC and explains the two verses by counting Jotham's twenty years from the start of his co-regency (751 BC) and Ahaz's twelve from his own co-regency (736 BC).

views.label: Shalmaneser
views.holders: 2 Kings 17:3-6 and 18:9-10; Babylonian Chronicle 1

argument.text: Kings names Shalmaneser as the king who besieged Samaria, and says “at the end of three years they took it”.

views.label: Sargon
views.holders: Sargon's own inscriptions

argument.text: Sargon lists the capture of Samaria among his deeds “from the year of my accession to the fifteenth year of my reign” (Luckenbill).

views.label: Shalmaneser's siege, Sargon's claim
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912), p. 323, following Winckler

argument.text: Rogers writes that Samaria fell in 722 “immediately on the death of Shalmaneser V”; “Sargon claims the victory for himself, though he could not have been present at all”, and the city “may have fallen while Shalmaneser still lived”.

views.label: Sabacon the Ethiopian
views.holders: James Ussher (1658), p. 68, citing Jerome's spelling “Sua”

argument.text: Ussher: “Which Sous or Sua, as Jerom calls him, seemeth to be none other but Sabacon the Ethiopian.”

notSaid: Kings does not say what became of Hoshea after he was imprisoned; there is no death, burial or “rest of the acts” for him.
Scripture gives no age or mother's name for Hoshea.
Kings does not name the Assyrian king who took the city in the ninth year; it says “the king of Assyria” (2 Kings 17:6).
